unit.title: Ratios and valuation
unit.description: P/E, PEG, EV/EBITDA, ROE, dividends, DCF and CAPE with real numbers

steps.title: What the P/E is
steps.body:
**P/E = price ÷ EPS** (or market cap ÷ net profit).

Panadería Global trades at €15 and its EPS is €0.975: **P/E = 15.4**. You're paying 15.4 times one year's earnings.

Its inverse is the **earnings yield**: 1 ÷ 15.4 = **6.5 %**, which you can compare with what a bond pays.

steps.title: How to read it
steps.body:
• The market's historical average is around **15-17**.
• **A low P/E doesn't mean cheap:** it could be a company in decline or one with a one-off inflated profit (from selling a building).
• **A high P/E doesn't mean expensive:** the company may be growing very fast.
• Compare it with its own **history** and its **sector**: a bank on a P/E of 8 and a software company on 35 can both be «fairly priced».

steps.title: Trailing and forward
steps.body: Using last year's earnings gives you the trailing P/E; using forecast earnings gives you the **forward P/E**. If earnings are set to grow a lot, the forward P/E will be lower.
steps.key: A P/E of 10 can be expensive and one of 30 cheap: it depends on what the company is going to earn.

steps.title: PEG: the P/E with growth
steps.body:
**PEG = P/E ÷ expected annual EPS growth (in %).**

Panadería Global: P/E of 15.4, growing at 8 % → PEG = **1.9**.

• Close to 1: reasonable.
• Above 2: expensive for its growth.

Two companies on a P/E of 20: if one grows at 20 % (PEG 1) and the other at 5 % (PEG 4), the first is cheaper.

steps.title: EV/EBITDA: debt included
steps.body:
**EV (enterprise value) = market cap + net debt.** It's what it would cost to buy the whole company, debts included.

Panadería Global: (1,500 + 320) ÷ 200 = **9.1**.

It lets you compare companies with different levels of debt, something the P/E can't see.

steps.title: P/B: for banks and insurers
steps.body:
**P/B = price ÷ book value per share.** Panadería Global: 15 ÷ 4.5 = **3.3**.

It's used mainly for banks and insurers, whose balance sheets are full of financial assets. For a software company, which is valued for its ideas rather than its assets, it tells you very little.
steps.key: Choose the ratio to suit the type of company.

u17l3.title: ROE and ROIC: is it a good business?

steps.title: ROE: the shareholder's return
steps.body:
**ROE = net profit ÷ shareholders' equity.**

Panadería Global: 97.5 ÷ 450 = **21.7 %**. For every €100 belonging to shareholders, it earns almost €22 a year.

An ROE above **15 %**, sustained over time, is very good.

steps.title: ROIC: the business's return
steps.body:
**ROIC = EBIT × (1 − tax) ÷ (equity + net debt).**

Panadería Global: 150 × 0.75 = 112.5; and 112.5 ÷ (450 + 320) = **14.6 %**.

It has to beat the **cost of capital** (≈ 8-10 %); otherwise the company grows while destroying value.

steps.title: The ROE trick
steps.body: With lots of debt, equity is small and ROE shoots up. ROIC includes debt, which makes it harder to inflate. The best businesses earn a lot on little capital and can **reinvest** at those rates for years.
steps.key: Look for businesses that turn every euro invested into much more than a euro, year after year.

steps.title: Two ratios
steps.body:
• **Dividend yield** = dividend per share ÷ price. Panadería Global pays €0.50 and trades at €15: **3.3 %**.
• **Payout ratio** = dividend ÷ EPS. 0.50 ÷ 0.975 = **51 %**: it pays out half and reinvests the other half.

steps.title: When a dividend is at risk
steps.body:
• **Payout ratio above 80-90 %** year after year, and even more so above 100 %: it's paying out more than it earns.
• **Dividend bigger than free cash flow:** it's being paid with debt.
• **Sky-high yield** (10 %, 12 %…): often it's because the price has collapsed and the market expects a cut.

steps.title: A dividend isn't a gift
steps.body: When a company pays €1 per share, the share usually falls by around €1 that day: the money moves from the company to your pocket, and Hacienda (the Spanish tax authority) takes its cut. What counts is the **total return**.
steps.key: A sustainable dividend comes out of cash, not out of debt.

steps.title: Bringing the future to today
steps.body:
A euro in 10 years' time is worth less than a euro today, because today you could invest it.

**Value today = future cash flow ÷ (1 + rate)^years**

At a rate of 9 %, €100 in a year's time is worth 100 ÷ 1.09 = **€91.74** today.

steps.title: Panadería Global's DCF
steps.body:
FCF of €1 per share, growing 6 % a year for 10 years and then 2 % forever. Discount rate: 9 %.

• Cash flows for years 1-10, discounted: ≈ **€8.6**
• Terminal value (Gordon formula): year 11 FCF ÷ (9 % − 2 %) ≈ €26.1; brought back to today: ≈ **€11.0**
• **Value ≈ €19.6.** It trades at €15: a 23 % margin.

steps.title: The lesson of DCF
steps.body:
Tweak the assumptions slightly:

• A 10 % rate: about **€17**.
• 4 % growth: about **€16.9**.
• Both at once: about **€14.7**, already below the price.

A DCF is a tool for **thinking** («what growth is the price assuming?»), not for producing an exact figure.
steps.key: If tweaking the assumptions slightly makes the value collapse, tread carefully.

steps.title: The P/E of the whole market
steps.body: The **CAPE** (or Shiller P/E) divides the price of an index by the **average earnings of the last 10 years**, adjusted for inflation. Because it uses 10 years, it smooths out the ups and downs of the economic cycle.

steps.title: The S&P 500 figures
steps.body:
• Average since 1871: about **17**.
• Peak: **44** in December 1999, just before the dot-com bubble burst.
• October 2026: around **41**, among the highest levels in history.

steps.title: What it tells you and what it doesn't
steps.body:
**Yes:** historically, a high CAPE has been linked to **lower returns over the following 10 years**.
**No:** it doesn't tell you **when** the market will fall; it can stay expensive for years.

Other regions trade at noticeably cheaper valuations: another argument for diversifying across countries.
steps.key: The CAPE is for adjusting your expectations, not for guessing next month.

u17l1-1.prompt: A share trades at €30 and its EPS is €2. What is its P/E?
u17l1-1.explanation: 30 ÷ 2 = 15: you're paying 15 years of current earnings.

u17l1-2.prompt: A company has a market cap of €4,000m and earns €250m a year. What is its P/E?
u17l1-2.explanation: 4,000 ÷ 250 = 16. It makes no difference whether you work it out per share or for the whole company.

u17l1-3.prompt: A share has a P/E of 20. What is its earnings yield?

u17l1-4.explanation: The share price divided by earnings per share.

u17l1-5.prompt: If EPS doubles and the price doesn't move, the P/E drops to ____ of what it was.
u17l1-5.explanation: The same price divided by twice the earnings gives half the P/E.

u17l1-6.prompt: A low P/E always means the share is cheap.
u17l1-6.explanation: It may reflect a company in decline or a one-off inflated profit.

u17l1-7.prompt: One year, a company sells its headquarters and its profit triples. Its P/E falls from 18 to 6. What has happened?
options: The P/E is distorted by a one-off profit
Its business has improved a lot
u17l1-7.explanation: That profit won't happen again: you need to look at recurring earnings.

u17l1-8.prompt: A share at €60 has EPS of €3 this year, and EPS of €4 is expected next year. What is its forward P/E?

u17l1-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Buy it now before it gets away
Look into why it's so low: a one-off profit, a business in decline or huge debt
A low P/E is always better
u17l1-10.explanation: A very low P/E is a question, not an answer.
feedback: Hold on: almost nothing has a P/E of 4 without a reason, and you need to find out what it is.
OK, I'll do my research before falling in love with the number.
Not always: sometimes it's the market's way of saying «this profit won't last».
lines: I've found a share with a P/E of 4 😍

u17l2-1.prompt: Match each company with the ratio most often used to analyse it.
options: An industrial company with lots of debt
u17l2-1.explanation: Each ratio sheds light on something different.

u17l2-2.prompt: P/E of 30 and expected EPS growth of 15 % a year. What is its PEG?

u17l2-3.prompt: Market cap of €2,000m, net debt of €600m and EBITDA of €260m. What is its EV/EBITDA?

u17l2-4.prompt: A bank trades at €6 and its book value per share is €7.5. What is its P/B?
u17l2-4.explanation: 6 ÷ 7.5 = 0.8: it trades below its book value.

u17l2-5.prompt: Two companies on a P/E of 20. A grows 20 % a year and B 5 %. Which is cheaper according to the PEG?
u17l2-5.explanation: The PEG relates the price to growth.

u17l2-6.prompt: Why is EV/EBITDA useful for comparing companies with different levels of debt?
options: Because it adds net debt to the company's value
Because it only looks at the dividend
u17l2-6.explanation: When you buy a whole company, you take on its debts too.

u17l2-7.prompt: Two companies with the same P/E can have very different EV/EBITDA ratios.
u17l2-7.explanation: If one has lots of debt, its EV is much larger than its market cap.

u17l2-8.prompt: A and B each have a market cap of €1,000m and EBITDA of €100m. A has no debt; B has €800m of net debt. A friend says they «cost the same». What do you tell them?
options: That B is cheaper because it has debt
That they're right: the market caps are the same
That B is more expensive: EV/EBITDA of 18 versus 10
u17l2-8.explanation: Enterprise value looks at the whole company, debt included.
feedback: Debt is something you owe, not a gift.
Market cap doesn't include debt: buy B and you also take on €800m that has to be paid back.

u17l2-9.prompt: Quick: P/E of 12 and 12 % growth. PEG?

u17l2-10.prompt: According to the PEG, reasonable or expensive for its growth?

u17l3-1.prompt: Net profit of €50m and shareholders' equity of €250m. What is the ROE?

u17l3-2.prompt: EBIT of €200m, 25 % tax, equity of €600m and net debt of €400m. What is the ROIC?

u17l3-3.prompt: A company earns €40m on equity of €400m (ROE of 10 %). It buys back shares with borrowed money: its equity drops to €200m and, because of the interest, its profit drops to €36m. What is its new ROE?
u17l3-3.explanation: 36 ÷ 200 = 18 %. ROE almost doubles without the business getting any better: it's the effect of the debt.

u17l3-4.prompt: An ROIC of 5 % with a 9 % cost of capital creates value.
u17l3-4.explanation: If ROIC doesn't beat the cost of capital, every euro reinvested destroys value.

u17l3-5.prompt: A very high ROE can be the result of the company having lots of debt.
u17l3-5.explanation: With little equity, any profit looks like a huge return.

u17l3-6.prompt: Why is ROIC more reliable than ROE for judging the business?
options: Because the tax authority calculates it
Because it includes debt in the capital
Because it always comes out higher
u17l3-6.explanation: ROE shoots up if the company takes on debt; ROIC, not so much.

u17l3-7.prompt: Quick: what sustained ROE is considered very good?
u17l3-7.explanation: As long as it doesn't come from excessive borrowing.

u17l3-8.prompt: Cost of capital: 9 %. Rank these from best to worst business by ROIC.
u17l3-8.explanation: Above 9 % it creates value; at 9 %, it neither creates nor destroys it; below that, it destroys it.

u17l3-9.prompt: Laura is comparing two companies. A: ROE of 25 % with net debt/EBITDA of 5. B: ROE of 18 %, no debt and an ROIC of 18 %. Which looks like the better business?
options: B: it earns a lot on all its capital without relying on debt
u17l3-9.explanation: Look at ROE alongside ROIC and debt.
feedback: With that much debt, the ROE may come from leverage more than from the business.
Exactly: an 18 % ROIC with no debt is a quality business.
With ROE, ROIC and debt you can already get a pretty good idea.

u17l3-10.prompt: A company with a 20 % ROIC reinvests all its profit at that rate for 10 years. By how much does its capital multiply? (one decimal place)
u17l3-10.explanation: 1.20¹⁰ ≈ 6.19. That's the idea behind «compounding machines»: an example, not a promise.

u17l4-1.prompt: A share trades at €40 and pays a dividend of €1.60 a year. What is its dividend yield?

u17l4-2.prompt: EPS of €2 and a dividend of €1.50. What is the payout ratio?
u17l4-2.explanation: 1.50 ÷ 2 = 75 %: it pays out three quarters of what it earns.

u17l4-3.prompt: Inditex proposed a dividend of €1.68 per share for its 2024 financial year. If the share traded at €48, what would its dividend yield be?
u17l4-3.explanation: 1.68 ÷ 48 = 3.5 %. It's a calculation using an example price, not a recommendation.

u17l4-4.prompt: Tick the messages that are signs of a scam or deception involving dividends.
options: The AGM approves a dividend of €0.50 per share, to be paid on 2 July.
I'll pay you a 3 % monthly «dividend» if you transfer your money to this account.
Live off dividends with €1,000: my course shows you how for €499.
🔥 Share with a 25 % ANNUAL dividend, GUARANTEED. Today only, limited places.
You've received €12.40 in dividends, net of withholding tax.
u17l4-4.explanation: Guaranteed returns, monthly «dividends» outside any regulated market and promises that you can live off your investments with €1,000 are classic signs of deception. At 4 %, €1,000 gives you about €40 a year.

u17l4-5.prompt: A company offers a 12 % dividend yield and its share price has fallen 50 % this year. What does that usually indicate?
options: That the market expects a dividend cut
That the company is doing very well
u17l4-5.explanation: The yield has gone up because the price has collapsed, not because they're paying more.

u17l4-6.prompt: A payout ratio of 110 % for three years in a row is sustainable.
u17l4-6.explanation: It's paying out more than it earns: it's dipping into cash or borrowing, and sooner or later it will have to cut.

u17l4-7.prompt: Bruno is comparing two shares by their dividend. A: 3.5 % yield, 50 % payout ratio and free cash flow that covers the dividend twice over. B: 9 % yield, 130 % payout ratio and rising debt. Which makes more sense?
options: It doesn't matter: dividends are guaranteed
Go for B: it pays almost three times as much
Go for A: its dividend is covered by earnings and cash
u17l4-7.explanation: Before looking at how much it pays, look at where the money comes from.
feedback: No share dividend is guaranteed.
It pays out more than it earns and borrows to do it: that 9 % could vanish overnight.
Exactly: a smaller but sustainable dividend is usually worth more than a high one that's at risk.

u17l4-9.prompt: A share is worth €30 and pays a dividend of €0.90. With no other news, at roughly what price does it usually open on the ex-dividend date?
u17l4-9.explanation: 30 − 0.90 = €29.10. The dividend comes out of the company's value.

u17l4-10.explanation: How much of the earnings is paid out.

u17l5-1.prompt: At a 10 % rate, how much is €110 that you'll receive in a year's time worth today?

u17l5-2.prompt: At an 8 % rate, how much is €1,000 that you'll receive in 5 years' time worth today?

u17l5-3.prompt: Terminal value with the Gordon formula: next year's FCF is €2, the discount rate is 9 % and perpetual growth is 2 %. What is it worth?

u17l5-4.prompt: Your DCF says a share is worth €25 and it trades at €20. What margin of safety do you have on the value?

u17l5-5.prompt: In a DCF, if you raise the discount rate, the estimated value…
u17l5-5.explanation: Future money is worth less today if you demand a higher return.

u17l5-6.prompt: What is a DCF mainly for?
options: Getting the exact value of a company
Knowing when the share price will go up
Thinking about what growth the price is assuming
u17l5-6.explanation: Small changes in the assumptions change the result a lot.

u17l5-7.prompt: In the Panadería Global example, raising the rate to 10 % and cutting growth to 4 % leaves the value below the €15 price.
u17l5-7.explanation: About €14.7: two reasonable tweaks eat up the whole margin of safety.

u17l5-8.prompt: Pablo does a DCF: a company trading at €60 is «worth» €120. To get there he assumed 25 % annual growth for 10 years and a 6 % rate. What should he do?
options: Go all in: it's worth double
Try more cautious assumptions and see how much the value changes
u17l5-8.explanation: A DCF is only as good as its assumptions.
feedback: His result depends on very optimistic assumptions: with more cautious ones, the «double» could disappear.
Good: if the value collapses with reasonable growth and a reasonable rate, the margin was an illusion.
Before convincing anyone else, convince yourself with cautious assumptions.

u17l5-9.prompt: A euro in 10 years' time is worth more than a euro today.
u17l5-9.explanation: It's worth less: today you could invest it and have it growing for 10 years.

u17l5-10.prompt: Put the steps of a simplified DCF in order.
options: Discount each cash flow back to today at your rate
Calculate the terminal value and discount it
Add it all up and compare it with the price
Estimate free cash flow for the coming years
u17l5-10.explanation: Future, discounting, terminal value and comparison.

u17l5-11.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Better to think in terms of a range and demand a good margin of safety
Perfect! If it trades at €47.31, it's cheap
u17l5-11.explanation: A DCF gives you a rough range, not an exact figure.
feedback: You're right: I move the rate by one point and get €40. Phew!
They're useful, for thinking. Not for giving you decimals.
One cent isn't a margin: your figure could be several euros out either way.
lines: My DCF says this share is worth exactly €47.32 🤓

u17l6-1.prompt: Look at the Nasdaq 100 from late 1997 to March 2000. What trend do you see? (Nasdaq 100 · weekly closes · up to 06/03/2000)
u17l6-1.explanation: A huge rise: valuations reached levels never seen before.

u17l6-2.prompt: March 2000: the S&P 500 CAPE has just hit its record (44, in December 1999) and the Nasdaq 100 has been soaring for years. What did the Nasdaq 100 do next?
u17l6-2.explanation: An extreme valuation tells you future returns will probably be low, but not when or by how much the price will move.

u17l6-3.prompt: November 1989: the Japanese stock market is trading at record valuations after a decade of euphoria. What did the Nikkei 225 do in the following years?
u17l6-3.explanation: As with the US CAPE, a very high valuation doesn't set a date: it only shifts the odds of what comes next.

u17l6-4.prompt: The CAPE divides the price by the average real earnings of the last ____ years.
u17l6-4.explanation: Ten years smooth out the economic cycle.

u17l6-5.prompt: What has the historical average of the S&P 500 CAPE been since 1871?
u17l6-5.explanation: In October 2026 it was around 41, well above that average.

u17l6-6.prompt: A very high CAPE tells you exactly when the market will fall.
u17l6-6.explanation: It can stay expensive for years; what it has been linked to is lower returns over 10 years.

u17l6-7.prompt: Historically, a high CAPE has been linked to lower returns over the following 10 years.
u17l6-7.explanation: Paying a high price leaves less room for gains afterwards.

u17l6-8.prompt: An index stands at 4,100 points and the average of its real earnings over 10 years is 100 points. What is its CAPE?

u17l6-9.prompt: With a CAPE of 41, what is the implied earnings yield (its inverse)?
u17l6-9.explanation: 1 ÷ 41 ≈ 2.44 %. With a CAPE of 17 it would be ≈ 5.9 %: paying more leaves a lower expected return.

u17l6-10.prompt: October 2026: the S&P 500 CAPE is around 41. Marta invests every month in a global index fund with a 25-year horizon. She reads that «the market is wildly expensive» and wants to sell everything. What would you tell her?
options: To buy more with borrowed money
To sell everything and wait for the crash
That a high CAPE suggests more modest expectations, not a crash date, and that she should calmly review her allocation and how she's diversified across countries
u17l6-10.explanation: The CAPE is for adjusting expectations and diversifying, not for jumping in and out of the market.
feedback: Borrowing in an expensive market piles risk on top of risk.
The CAPE doesn't say when: she'd have to get both the exit and the re-entry right.
Good: a global fund already includes cheaper regions, and her plan runs for 25 years.

u17l6-11.prompt: Quick: what was the S&P 500's highest ever CAPE?
u17l6-11.explanation: December 1999, just before the dot-com bubble burst.
